# Judging *The Time Machine* (Chapters I–VI) as an explanation

**1. The question, frozen.** The piece opens with the Time Traveller "expounding a recondite matter," and everything after serves one explanation: **Time is a fourth dimension of Space, so a machine can travel through it.** That is the central question (the text heads for a chapter called "Time Travelling"), so I freeze on it and hold it. Range: any real body, any time. Kind: a case for a possibility (*why it can be done*), resting on a demonstration (the model vanishing). I keep the question still throughout.

**2. The explanation in parts** (his own words).
P1 "a mathematical line… has no real existence… neither has a mathematical plane."
P2 "Can a cube that does not last for any time at all have a real existence?"
P3 "any real body must have extension in four directions: Length, Breadth, Thickness, and Duration."
P4 "There is no difference between Time and any of the three dimensions of Space except that our consciousness moves along it."
P5 "We are always getting away from the present moment… passing along the Time-Dimension with a uniform velocity."
P6 "why should he not hope that he may be able to stop or accelerate his drift… or even turn about?"
P7 the balloon/gravitation analogy ("Gravitation limits us there… balloons").
P8 the machine (levers, saddle, forward and reverse).
P9 the vanishing demonstration + "presentation below the threshold, diluted presentation."
P10 "Into the future or the past—I don't, for certain, know which."

**3. Part by part.** (One mark each; never added up.)

| Part | Mark | Because |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | idle | I removed it in a group with P2; the argument still reaches P3. It clears ground but carries nothing. |
| P2 | held | Removing it loses the duration requirement — a job not in doubt. |
| P3 | loose | "Duration as a direction like length" swaps cleanly for "things persist through time," which does the same job and supports no travel. |
| P4 | held if | It does the central job, but what holds it is the demonstration (P9), which is itself in doubt. |
| P5 | loose | Persistence renamed "drift." Swap "drift" for "persist" and nothing breaks. |
| P6 | held if | Held only by P5 and P7, both loose. |
| P7 | loose | Swap gravity/balloons for any other limit ("we can't fly like birds — yet we built aeroplanes") and it works as well. |
| P8 | held if | Built and minded, but its working is asserted, not shown. |
| P9 | held, with a loose patch | The vanishing is the one thing that could have failed — so it does work — but "diluted presentation" is a soft patch (gauge: the 50–100× speed ratio). |
| P10 | loose | A catch-all over direction that widens the claim so nothing can catch it out. |

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**
- **Flip.** Had the model *not* vanished, the theory fails — good. But P10 shows the habit of widening instead.
- **Direction.** The vanishing is evidence *for* time travel, sold as proof *of* it. A vanishing could be produced otherwise — the Medical Man supplies the rival himself (the Christmas ghost). So a backward step is dressed as production.
- **Answer in the starting points.** "We are always getting away from the present moment" *is* the conclusion (movement in time) under the name "drift." Found and flagged.
- **Jobs and their origin.** The strongest jobs are the audience's — indeed **given**, not set by himself: "why cannot we move about in Time?" (Medical Man); "it must have gone into the past" (Psychologist). That makes the fit meaningful. "Why not another direction at right angles" is his own and is **added**.
- **Pairs that pull.** P4 ("no difference") fights P5 ("one direction") — the arrow. It also fights his own "a fixed and unalterable thing," the Four-Dimensioned man: if a whole life is a fixed block, it can be *read off*, not *travelled*. The line is drawn at "our consciousness moves along it," and a true reversal would show it wrong.
- **Catch-alls.** Two: "diluted presentation" (a rough gauge) and "future or past" (no gauge at all).
- **What the change list leaves out.** The arrow of time, the machine's mechanism, the destination — silently.
- **Rival.** The conjuring trick is properly built and properly answered (the worn body of Chapter III). This is the account's strongest moment.
- **Where the parts came from.** P3–P4 **borrowed** from the fourth-dimension geometry of Hinton and Newcomb (Newcomb cited); P8 **built**; P9 **fitted** on a single trial.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.** Fix the direction (say where it went); give a mechanism with a dial you could turn to change *which* year; say why we remember the past and not the future; and put a gauge on "diluted presentation."

**6. What this does not show.** Hard to vary is not the same as true. A tight account can still be false, and a genuine trick can be tight and true-as-trick.

**7. One next step.** Before the next demonstration, write down what would be seen if it were *not* time travel, and turn "future or past" into a prediction that could be checked.
